name: FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data)
publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
description: Around 800,000 economic time series -- US and international -- collected from about 100 statistical agencies and served under one identifier scheme. If a macro number has a name (UNRATE, CPIAUCSL, GDP, DGS10) it has a FRED series id, and every series comes with its units, seasonal adjustment, frequency and the agency that actually produced it. ALFRED, the sibling archive, keeps the vintages: what a series said on a given day, before revision.
geography: US, plus international series sourced from OECD, IMF, World Bank and national statistics offices

temporal.start: 1776 for a few annual series; most monthly series start 1947-1960
temporal.grain: daily to annual, varies by series
temporal.updated: on the releasing agency's schedule, usually within minutes of publication

license.name: mostly public domain (US federal sources); some series are copyrighted by their originating provider
license.redistribution: check the per-series 'Copyright' notice on the series page before republishing values -- most are free to reuse, but the licensed feeds (S&P, some OECD) are not

access.auth_note: the JSON/XML API at api.stlouisfed.org needs a free key from https://fredaccount.stlouisfed.org/apikeys. The CSV download at fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv needs no key at all -- see the gotchas.
access.size_hint: one series as CSV is a few KB to a few hundred KB; the full-catalogue bulk zip is ~100 MB
access.rate_limit: 120 requests per minute per key (documented); the keyless fredgraph CSV route has no published limit, so throttle yourself
access.pagination: limit / offset, default 1000, max 1000 on list endpoints

probes.description: A whole series as CSV, with no API key
probes.note: Also pins the April 2020 unemployment spike (14.8) as a value check, so a route that answers 200 with the wrong series fails here.

probes.description: The documented API without a key -- proves the gate is where we say it is
probes.note: A clean 400 with a readable message, not a redirect to an HTML page. Compare census-acs, which 302s a keyless call into a 200 HTML error and breaks JSON parsers silently.

gotchas.trap: Everyone reaches for the API key first, because that is what the docs lead with. For 'give me this series' you do not need one.
gotchas.fix: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=SERIES returns the full history as CSV, keyless, and takes id=A,B,C to align several series on one date column plus cosd/coed for a window. Get a key when you need to *search* the catalogue or read series metadata; skip it when you already know the id.

gotchas.trap: The CSV's first column header is `observation_date`. A great deal of published code -- and most tutorials written before it changed -- does df['DATE'] and dies with a KeyError.
gotchas.fix: Read the header rather than hard-coding it, or index positionally. Observed 2026-09-10.

gotchas.trap: Two series that look like the same measure often differ in seasonal adjustment or units, and nothing in the id says so. CPIAUCSL is seasonally adjusted; CPIAUCNS is not.
gotchas.fix: Read `units`, `seasonal_adjustment_short` and `frequency` from /fred/series before comparing anything. The `_NS` / `SL` suffix convention is a habit, not a rule.

gotchas.trap: FRED serves the *current* value of a series, so a backtest built on it is quietly using numbers nobody had at the time. GDP gets revised for years.
gotchas.fix: Use ALFRED -- /fred/series/observations with realtime_start and realtime_end -- when the question is 'what did we believe on date X'. This is the single most common way an economic backtest is wrong.

gotchas.trap: Not everything on FRED is public domain, despite the .org and the federal publisher.
gotchas.fix: Series sourced from licensed providers carry a copyright notice on their series page. Check before republishing the values themselves; citing the id is always fine.

fields: series_id -- the whole key space; UNRATE, CPIAUCSL, GDP, DGS10, PAYEMS
seasonal_adjustment_short -- 'SA' or 'NSA'; comparing across this is a common error
frequency_short -- D, W, M, Q, A
realtime_start / realtime_end -- the ALFRED vintage window, not the observation date
last_updated -- when the series itself last changed, useful for cache invalidation
